sections.title_en: 1. The Mitzva of Building a Synagogue
sections.body_en:
Wherever ten Jews live, it is a mitzva for them to set aside a house in which they will gather for prayer and Torah, and this house is called a synagogue (beit knesset). The synagogue has two main purposes: first, to help the orderly holding of the prayers and the Torah reading; second, to serve as a 'small sanctuary' that extends the holiness of the Temple to the community. As it is said (Shemot 25:8): "And let them make Me a sanctuary, that I may dwell among them". And although the main intention of the verse is to instruct the building of the Temple, a branch that extends from this mitzva is the mitzva to build a synagogue. For the purpose of both is one: to set aside a house for the service of God and the dwelling of His Shekhina in Israel.

Especially after our Temple was destroyed and we were exiled from our land, and the Shekhina too went into exile with us, the need for the synagogue grew. As it is said (Yeḥezkel 11:16): "Therefore say: Thus says the Lord God: Although I have removed them far off among the nations, and although I have scattered them among the countries, yet I have been to them a small sanctuary in the countries where they have come". Rabbi Yitzḥak said (Megilla 29a): "Yet I have been to them a small sanctuary… – these are the synagogues and study halls", for the holiness that dwells in the synagogue is akin to the holiness that dwells in the Temple. And likewise the prayers said in the synagogue were instituted corresponding to the sacrifices that were offered in the Temple. And Rava expounded the verse (Tehillim 90:1): "Lord, You have been our dwelling place in all generations", as referring to "synagogues and study halls", through which God causes His Shekhina to dwell in Israel in all the generations (see above 12:1).

Just as there were synagogues in the time of the Second Temple, so too after the Third Temple is built, speedily in our days, the synagogues will remain to serve as a 'small sanctuary' for each and every community. And even the synagogues in the Diaspora will go up to the Land, as the Sages said (Megilla 29a): "The synagogues and study halls in Babylonia are destined to be established in the Land of Israel". Thus in the future too, after the Temple is built, the synagogues will serve as a 'small sanctuary' for each and every community, and through them the holiness of the Temple will extend in miniature to each community, and as a result all Israel will be strengthened to fulfil their destiny of revealing the word of God and His blessing in the world.1

notes_en.en:
Some say that we do not find a mitzva from the Torah or from the words of the Sages to build a synagogue; rather, it is a 'communal enactment' for the needs of the public, which is enforced (Yad Yamin, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3). And many hold that it is a rabbinic mitzva to build a synagogue (Ḥikrei Lev 3, Yoreh De'ah 114; Sefer Ḥayim of R. Ḥayim Palagi 45:7; Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:3, according to the view of the Rambam; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 42). And some hold that it is a mitzva from the Torah, and it is a branch of the mitzva to build the Temple (Neḥmad Le-Mar'eh, Pe'ah chapter 8, 42b). And so it is implied by the Zohar (Ra'aya Meheimna, Beshalaḥ 59b), and so it appears from the words of the Yere'im (above 12, note 1). And R. Shlomo Kluger inclined to this (Shenot Ḥayim part 2, Peret Ve-Olelot 1), and explained that for this reason it is forbidden to demolish a synagogue before building a new one. And he discussed whether the mitzva is rabbinic, as a remembrance of the Temple, or from the Torah, for the sake of prayer, corresponding to the two purposes I wrote above.
Even in the time of the Temple there was a synagogue near it on the Temple Mount, as brought in Yoma (68b), and Rashi. And there were likewise synagogues throughout the Land (Rambam in his Commentary on the Mishna, Ta'anit 4:3). And so he wrote in the Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:44), that even in the time of the Temple there was a mitzva to build synagogues in other places for those who could not come to the Temple, so that they would pray in them. See further Har Tzvi (Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:84). It stands to reason that following the building of the Temple, the revelation of holiness in the whole world, including in the synagogues in the Land and abroad – will intensify.

sections.body_en:
Since it is a mitzva for every community to build itself a synagogue, all the members of the community are obligated to take part in financing its building and its upkeep. Likewise, it is a mitzva that the synagogue also serve as a study hall for Torah study, and it is a mitzva to establish Torah lessons in it, and to set up in it a library of sacred books in all areas of the Torah, so that those who come to the synagogue can study from them. When the synagogue is not suitable for this, the members of the community are obligated to set up a study hall (Biur Halakha 150:1, s.v. 'Ve-likno'). Women too have an optional mitzva to pray in the synagogue, and in practice many women are accustomed to attend the synagogue from time to time – therefore women too are obligated to take part in financing the building of the synagogue.2

Generally the division of payments was determined according to wealth – the rich paid more and the poor less (Shulḥan Arukh 53:23). However, some communities established an equal payment for every person who prays in the synagogue, and some communities were accustomed to finance its building by selling its seats, the front seats being sold at a higher price, and each person decided which seat he wished to buy (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 150:2). Members of a community who are not able to finance the building of a synagogue must rent a place for prayer for themselves, and when they become wealthy they should build a permanent synagogue (Mishna Berura 150:2).

There is a virtue for one who lives near the synagogue, as the Sages said (Bava Metzia 107a): "'Blessed shall you be in the city' (Devarim 28:3) – that your house will be near the synagogue". And likewise it is related of the house of Oved-Edom the Gittite that it was blessed after the Ark of God rested near his house (II Shmuel 6:11-12). However, one who lives far from the synagogue also has a virtue, in the reward for the steps of walking to it (Bava Metzia there).

notes_en.en:
Tosefta (Bava Metzia 11:23): "The people of a town compel one another to build themselves a synagogue and to buy themselves a Torah scroll and the Prophets". And so wrote the Rif (Bava Batra 8b), the Rosh (there 1:24), the Rambam (Laws of Neighbours 6:1) and the Shulḥan Arukh (Ḥoshen Mishpat 163:1). And so wrote, concerning a synagogue, the Rambam (Laws of Prayer 11:1) and the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 150:1). The Rema wrote (Ḥoshen Mishpat 163:1) that the minority may compel the majority for known communal needs. Included in this is the upkeep of the synagogue and its expansion when necessary (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan, Ḥoshen Mishpat 163:1).
In the Biur Halakha (150:1, s.v. 'Ve-likno') he proved from the law of compulsion to buy books of the Tanakh that if the public has no place to study, "they compel one another to build a study hall, for what benefit is there in buying books if they have no place to study". And so wrote our master Rav Kook (Igrot Ha-Re'aya 4, 5678, 371), and added that the study hall takes precedence over the synagogue. Included in the mitzva is buying all the books required for Torah study (Mishna Berura 150:3; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 1; see above 8:4). And this obligation takes precedence over beautifying the synagogue (Ḥesed La-Alafim 150:1).
The Maharam Mintz (7) wrote, and it is brought in the Darkhei Moshe (Ḥoshen Mishpat 163:2), concerning financing a mikveh, that even older women must take part in financing it, since it is needed by the whole public. Moreover, they too sometimes immerse in preparation for the Days of Awe. Until here. All the more so women are obligated to take part in financing a synagogue, since they attend it more often. And see Mikdash Me'at (of Rav Druk, siman 2). When it concerns a neighbourhood or a settlement that has several synagogues, a person cannot be obligated to take part in financing a particular synagogue; rather, whoever joins a community is obligated to take part in financing its synagogue.

sections.title_en: 3. The Unity of the Community in the Synagogue
sections.body_en:
When the synagogue is too small to hold all the worshippers, and it cannot be enlarged, it is a mitzva to set up another synagogue (Magen Avraham 154:23). But if there is room in the synagogue for all the worshippers, and there is no significant reason of value to set up another synagogue, it is forbidden to divide the community. And one who donates to setting up such a synagogue has in his hand not a mitzva but a transgression, because unity is a supreme value in Israel. As the Sages said (Devarim Rabba 5:10), when Israel are united, even if there are grave sins among them, the Holy One, blessed be He, helps them to defeat their enemies. But when there is division among them, even though they have many mitzvot to their credit, the Holy One, blessed be He, does not help them, and they are smitten before their enemies. And even the name 'beit knesset' (house of gathering) is called after unity, for everyone gathers in it together. In addition, the greater the number of worshippers, the more the honour of Heaven is magnified, as it is said (Mishlei 14:28): "In the multitude of people is the king's glory" (Meshiv Davar 1:46; Mishpetei Uziel 3:19).

Experience too shows that people connected to a large and stable community receive from it more support and strengthening in days of joy and sorrow. In addition, a large community is able to organise more Torah lessons and acts of kindness, and its members can rise higher in Torah and good deeds. And even the children who grow up in a large and strong community remember more fondly the prayers of the synagogue and the fellowship of the worshippers, and when they grow up they are more eager to continue in the way of Torah and mitzvot.

Therefore, although it is possible that some people would feel more comfortable in a small minyan that would conduct itself according to their inclination, or in which they could serve more often as ḥazanim, it is preferable that they give up their wish in order to preserve the unity of the community.

However, when the urge for dispute intensifies and words of moral rebuke do not help, and the members of the community sink into disputes and sin with quarrels, it is preferable that they sin less, and separate and set up another synagogue (Mishna Berura 150:2, following the Radbaz 3:472).

Sometimes the arguments are not personal but stem from different emphases in the style of prayer, and then it may be fitting to set up several minyanim within the framework of the community: one for those who want to lengthen the prayer in order to concentrate more, one for those who want to shorten it so as not to burden the public, and one for those who want to sing much and involve the youth in the prayer. For unlike the value of 'unity', which overrides many other values, the value of "in the multitude of people is the king's glory" does not override other values, but must be integrated with them in balance. However, even when it is right to set up minyanim suited to the different shades within the community, one must strive for the unity of the community in Torah lessons and joint prayers. For this purpose it is very desirable that the community have a rabbi who will take part in shaping the various minyanim, and will strive together with the whole public for the unity of the community.

Similarly, sometimes the need to separate stems from differences of nusaḥ. For example, the existing minyan follows a certain nusaḥ, and in the meantime the minyan has grown and includes many who have a different nusaḥ. Or at first they were accustomed to combine two nusaḥim, and when the worshippers increased, many of them preferred to pray the whole prayer in the nusaḥ of their fathers. In these cases too it is right to consult the local rabbi, so that on the one hand each person can pray in the nusaḥ of his fathers, and on the other hand the community will remain united; for example, that the two synagogues be in the same compound, so that the Torah lessons and joyous occasions of both will be shared by all (see Peninei Halakha, Prayer 6:6).3

notes_en.en:
In the Magen Avraham (154:23) he brought from the Rivash (253) that one who prevents the building of a new synagogue, even when there is a synagogue in the town, prevents the public from performing a mitzva. However, the Magen Avraham explained that if the first synagogue holds the public – it is forbidden to separate. And so wrote Ḥayei Adam (17:45). And so wrote the Netziv (Meshiv Davar 1:46): "Separation where there is no necessity – is a great transgression, as it is written (Yeshayahu 57:13): When you cry out, let your assemblies deliver you; and the larger the assembly – the more the prayer is heard, and ten praying together are not like a hundred performing one mitzva and glorifying the King of the world. And in Bereshit Rabba chapter 4 it is stated that 'that it was good' was not said on the second day because of the separation of the waters, and Rabbi Tavyomi said: If a division that is for the existence of the world has no 'that it was good' in it, a division that is for the confusion of the world all the more so; and the meaning of division here is not a dispute but a separation between things that cleave together, like the dividing of the waters, even if they do not quarrel and contend with one another". And so wrote Mishpetei Uziel (7:19): "There is no permission to make temporary or even permanent synagogues in private rooms… in a place where there are public synagogues, for all such synagogues diminish the image of the synagogue in its splendour and perfection, and also in its inner improvement… as it is written: In the multitude of people is the king's glory, and every diminishing of the image of the synagogue is included in disparagement of the synagogue and separation from the public". And so wrote Beit Shlomo (Oraḥ Ḥayim 26), that one should not separate for the sake of extra comfort or honour: "If the study hall holds them all, and their hearts too are at peace with the people of the study hall – they are forbidden to separate, if their intention is only to have a roomier place to pray, or because of imagined honour and other weak reasons, which are not worth it against the honour of the Omnipresent, blessed be He and blessed be His Name, for in the multitude of people is the king's glory". And one wrote that it is fitting to be stringent not to separate even when the place does not hold them all (Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:21). On the other hand, one wrote that it is permitted to separate and set up a new place even when there is no strong reason (Yaskil Avdi part 4, Oraḥ Ḥayim 12).
The Maharam Schick (Ḥoshen Mishpat 23) wrote that it is permitted to separate for the sake of praying in the nusaḥ of one's fathers or according to special kavanot. And so wrote the Maharsham (3:168), on condition that the first minyan is not cancelled. And in the Avnei Nezer (Oraḥ Ḥayim 36) he permitted dividing when there is "a proper reason" for it. And in the Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:46) he permitted dividing and setting up a minyan for people who live far away, so that more people would merit to pray with a minyan. Until here. And likewise it is permitted to divide in order to set up a synagogue that is faithful to the values of the Torah, for example where in the existing synagogue they disregard the mitzva of settling the Land and the unity of Israel, and in the new one they will appoint a rabbi who educates towards this.

sections.title_en: 4. The Location of the Synagogue at the Height of the Town
sections.body_en:
Since the synagogue is a 'small sanctuary', it is the most important of the houses of the town. In order to give expression to this, the Sages ruled (Tosefta Megilla 3:14) to build it in the highest place in the area – "at the height of the town", as it is said (Mishlei 1:21): "She calls at the head of the noisy streets". In the past a small settlement was called a 'town', and then the instruction was to set up the synagogue on the highest place in the settlement. When settlements expanded and grew until many synagogues needed to be built in them, the instruction was that each synagogue be built in the place that is high relative to the area near it.

The Sages further said (Shabbat 11a): "Any town whose roofs are higher than the synagogue – will in the end be destroyed, as it is said (Ezra 9:9): to raise up the house of our God, and to restore its ruins". God gives life and content to a person, and when the synagogue is raised above the other houses, the community is connected to the source of life and is blessed. But when the various needs receive the high place, they become the main thing, and since they have no eternal value, the town will in the end be destroyed.

Therefore, one must take care that the synagogue be the highest of the houses of the town. And if a person built his house higher than the synagogue, he is obligated to lower his house so that it will be lower than the synagogue, or to raise the synagogue above his house (Rosh, Shabbat 1:23; Shulḥan Arukh 150:2-3). And if he does not do so, it turns out that he is arrogant and insolent towards Heaven, and his sin is great.

During the exile, in many places they forbade the Jews to build a synagogue in the highest place in the town, and likewise forbade raising its height, and then they were forced to lower the height of the synagogue, and sometimes they even had to conceal it on a ground floor beneath a residential building (Beit Yosef 154:1; Rema 150:2). In practice the poskim wrote that when the gentiles build their houses higher than the synagogue, it is not possible for the synagogue to be the highest of the houses, and therefore there is no prohibition for Jews to raise their houses higher than it; but they must take care to honour the interior of the synagogue as far as they can, so that it will be the most honoured of the houses of Israel (Magen Avraham 150:2; Mishna Berura 5, and others).

In recent generations the human population has grown greatly, and many live in high-rise buildings. If people wish the synagogue to be the highest of the houses, they would need to build it on the top floor of the highest building in the area, and then it would be very difficult to go up to it. And if they wished the whole public to live in low houses, the cost of housing would skyrocket. And it is clear that the Sages did not intend this enactment to become the most expensive of all the mitzvot of the Torah; rather, their intention was that if in any case all the houses are one or two storeys high, the synagogue should be raised above all the houses.

Therefore, the meaning of the mitzva today is that it is a mitzva to build the synagogue in an honourable and splendid manner, inside and out, more than the residential houses of the members of the community. And that the height of the interior space of the synagogue be higher than the interior space of the public and cultural buildings in the area, in order to show and make tangible that the synagogue is the most important and honoured. Likewise, it is a mitzva to allot to the synagogue a fine plot, and one should try that it be in the highest place in that area, so that those going to the synagogue will go up to it. However, when the neighbourhood or settlement is built on a slope, it is preferable to allot to the synagogue a plot in the centre of the neighbourhood or settlement, so that it will be easy for everyone to walk to it, even though it will not be in the highest place (Mor U-Ketzi'a 150).4

notes_en.en:
The Sages said (Shabbat 11a): "Any town whose roofs are higher than the synagogue will in the end be destroyed, as it is said (Ezra 9:9): to raise up the house of our God, and to restore its ruins. And this applies only to houses, but with kashkushei and avrurei – we have no concern", that they may be higher than the synagogue. According to the Arukh and the Ran, kashkushei and avrurei are watchtowers for the town, and since they need to be built high, it is permitted to raise them above the synagogue. But domes intended for beauty may not be raised above the synagogue. Therefore, when there is a great need to build high-rise buildings for housing and offices, there is no prohibition, since they are built for a need and not for splendour. And so wrote the Me'iri (Shabbat 11a), that there is no prohibition when the houses are raised not "in the way of dominion but in order to increase dwellings and upper storeys".
However, according to Rashi, the Rosh, the Tur and the Shulḥan Arukh (150:2), 'kashkushei and avrurei' are domes and sloping roofs intended for beauty, and since they are not used, there is no prohibition that they be higher than the synagogue. According to their view, it would seemingly be forbidden to build houses and offices above the height of the synagogue. But in today's reality, the cost of lowering the houses would be enormous, both in the need to buy land and in doubling the price of apartments, and it is clear that the Sages did not intend to establish such an expensive enactment. Therefore, the fulfilment of the mitzva is in allotting an honourable area to the synagogue. Likewise, it is a mitzva to build the synagogue with more honour and splendour than the other houses of the neighbourhood, as brought in the Zohar (Ra'aya Meheimna, Beshalaḥ 59b) and in Sefer Ḥasidim (535). And so wrote the Rambam (Laws of Things Forbidden on the Altar 7:11): "If he built a house of prayer – it should be finer than his dwelling house"; and so wrote his son Rabbi Avraham (Ha-Maspik Le-Ovdei Hashem, chapter 25), Rav Auerbach (Oraḥ Ne'eman 150:2) and Alei Tamar (Shekalim 5:4). In the mitzva to honour the synagogue more than the other public and cultural buildings in the area, the intention is relative to buildings intended for the use of a similar number of people; but when they built a hall for an audience of thousands of people, or when they set up a mall for many shops, it is natural that they will be larger than the synagogue, since they serve more people.

sections.title_en: 5. The Holy Ark and the Bima
sections.body_en:
In order to honour the Torah scroll, people are accustomed to build a fine ark for it, and they place the ark at the front of the synagogue, and try to beautify and adorn it as much as possible, and they call it: 'the Holy Ark' (Aron Ha-Kodesh) (Shabbat 32a; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 282:1). Some enhance by raising the Holy Ark so that one goes up to it by steps. When possible, the raised area is widened so that the kohanim can stand on it for the Priestly Blessing.

People are accustomed to fix the place of the Holy Ark on the side facing Jerusalem, so that those standing in prayer and facing towards Jerusalem will also face towards the Holy Ark. If because of constraints or by mistake they fixed the Holy Ark on another side, they should face towards Jerusalem in prayer (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 150:5; 94:1-2; Magen Avraham; Mishna Berura 9-10).5

People are accustomed to cover the Holy Ark with a parokhet, as an expression of the need to balance the excessive longing to draw near to the sacred by adding modesty and concealment of the sanctified Torah scroll. And as it is said concerning the Mishkan (Shemot 26:33): "and the veil shall divide for you between the holy place and the most holy" (Zera Emet part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 26). However, there were communities in which people were accustomed to make very beautiful doors for the Holy Ark without a parokhet, and they preferred to enhance the honour of the ark rather than keep the enhancement of the custom of the parokhet.6

Many are accustomed to adorn the Holy Ark with the shape of the two Tablets of the Covenant, in order to recall the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai. Many are accustomed to make the upper side of the tablets rounded, and one should not cast aspersions on their custom, for great and good people were accustomed so (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 15:9). Likewise many are accustomed to adorn the Holy Ark or the parokhet with the shape of lions, in order to express thereby the kingship of God, that even the lion, king of the beasts, gives honour to its Creator, like the curtains in the Mishkan in which the shape of lions was woven. However, among those of Sephardi origin, many refrain from this (there 15:8).

Pictures that are not usually fixed in the synagogue, including pictures of rabbis, may not be fixed in the synagogue. And even pictures that it was customary to paint in the synagogue, in order to express the song of the created beings to their Creator, or corresponding to the twelve signs of the zodiac, since not everyone is accustomed to them, they should be fixed above the height of a person, so that they will not distract the worshippers (Shulḥan Arukh 90:20; Magen Avraham; Mishna Berura 71; Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 15:8).

A fine bima is placed in the middle of the synagogue, like the altar that was in the middle of the Mishkan, and the Torah is read on it (Ḥatam Sofer 1:28; Meshiv Davar 1:15). Many of those of Sephardi origin are accustomed that the ḥazan too stands near the bima, whereas those of Ashkenazi origin are accustomed that the ḥazan stands near the Holy Ark, and only when the synagogue is very large does the ḥazan stand by the bima so that everyone can hear him. Following the custom of the Reform to place the bima at the front of the synagogue, like churches, the Ashkenazi communities became more insistent that the bima be in the middle of the synagogue. And a debate arose whether when necessary, such as in small synagogues, one may place the bima near the Holy Ark, or whether it is forbidden because of 'the statutes of the gentiles' (see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 28:8).

notes_en.en:
According to many, even when from the point of view of the architectural plan there is great benefit in building the synagogue in such a way that the Holy Ark is not on the side of Jerusalem, one should give up the benefit and build it towards Jerusalem (Ha-Elef Lekha Shlomo, Oraḥ Ḥayim 48; Maharam Schick, Oraḥ Ḥayim 47; Meshiv Davar 1:10; Aḥiezer 3:79, and others). However, the exact angle may be given up in case of need (Halikhot Shlomo, Prayer 19:4, note 14). On the other hand, some are lenient when necessary to plan the synagogue so that the Holy Ark will not be towards Jerusalem, and they instruct the public to stand in the Amida towards Jerusalem (Peri Megadim 94, Eshel Avraham 3; Responsa Mahara"v 2:15). And so wrote R. Yosef Mashash (Mayim Ḥayim 2:109), and testified that so they were accustomed in many places in Morocco.
In practice, when the Holy Ark is not on the side of Jerusalem, many mistakenly pray towards the ark. Despite this, some say that one should not be drawn after them, but must pray towards Jerusalem (Yad Eliyahu 1; Ḥesed La-Alafim 94:4). And some say that it is preferable not to separate from the public, but to pray with them while turning slightly towards Jerusalem (Mishna Berura 10; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 13).

A cloth parokhet is mentioned in Megilla (26b), and it is called a 'perisa'. In Zera Emet (part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 26) he wrote that it is not fitting to abolish the custom of the parokhet, which is intended for modesty, like the parokhet of the Mishkan and like the service garments that covered the vessels of the Mishkan when they were transported. And so wrote the Maḥazik Berakha (154:3) and Sha'arei Teshuva (154:10). And so wrote Shomer Emet (5:18), but noted that in Tunis they were not accustomed to fix a parokhet. Until here. According to Rashi and most Rishonim (Megilla there), they spread the parokhet on the inner side of the ark, and according to Tosafot (there, s.v. 'Merish') outside. In practice, the prevalent custom is to fix a parokhet outside the Holy Ark. And some even held that one must be particular about this (Yeḥaveh Da'at 6:9). However, there are communities that kept the custom by placing the parokhet inside, and there is no flaw in their custom (Aseh Lekha Rav 2:26). And those who wish to forgo the parokhet altogether may do so, for from the fact that most halakhic books did not mention this custom, it follows that it is not obligatory.

sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Tosefta Megilla 3:14) that the proper seating arrangement in the synagogue is that the whole congregation sits row after row with their faces towards the Holy Ark and Jerusalem, and in the first row the elders would sit with "their faces towards the people and their backs towards the sacred" (Rif, Rosh, Megilla 3:11; Rambam, Laws of Prayer 11:4; Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 150:5). In practice, the Holy Ark is in the centre of the wall at the front of the synagogue, and the elders sit on both its sides, with their backs to the wall at the front of the synagogue.

The elders who sat facing the people were the Torah sages, as the Sages said: "An elder (zaken) is only one who has acquired wisdom" (Kiddushin 32b; Sifra, Kedoshim). And they were called 'elders' because naturally, when people were accustomed to dedicate the Shabbatot and festivals to Torah study, and also on weekdays fixed times for Torah, the elders, who had managed to study Torah over more years and to accumulate more life experience, were the wiser in understanding the Torah.

By seating the elders at the front of the synagogue, the whole public gave honour to the Torah and its sages, and thereby intensified the desire to engage in Torah, to walk in the ways of God and to add goodness and blessing to the world. In addition, by the sages' facing the people, the sages expressed honour for all who come to the synagogue, God's beloved children, who came to pray before Him and to study His Torah (see Beit Yosef 150:5; Har Tavor 7).

In practice, although in many communities people were accustomed to keep this custom, there were communities in which they did not keep it. Apparently there were two main reasons for this. First, sometimes it is difficult to determine who the Torah sages of the community are, and the attempt to decide this is liable to lead to disputes, and they preferred to avoid it. Second, in places where they found it difficult to maintain the synagogue from the community's taxes, they maintained it by selling the seats to the worshippers, and the honoured seats at the front of the synagogue were sold to the highest bidder and not left for the Torah sages.

In the period of the Aḥaronim, in many synagogues of those of Sephardi origin they abolished the custom of the elders sitting facing the people, and seated the rabbis in the centre beside the bima, with the whole congregation facing the bima, and in this way everyone was united together in prayer and song around the rabbis and the ḥazan. This form of seating of the congregation also existed in some of the synagogues in Ashkenaz.

However, it seems that concerning seating the elders at the front of the synagogue it is fitting to return to the original custom, in order to honour the Torah and increase its influence. And they should take care to seat there elders who are faithful to all the mitzvot and values of the Torah of Israel: Torah study and settling the Land, mitzvot between man and God and mitzvot between man and his fellow, and derekh eretz, which preceded the Torah. In order to emphasise the whole range of values in the Torah, it is right to seat at the front of the synagogue also elders who are Torah-observant and have attained achievements in science, in settling the Land and in the army, for they too are included among the elders whom it is fitting to honour so that they will serve as an example for the young.

Even in a place where the elders are not seated facing the public, at the very least it is right to seat the rabbi there, and thereby they will fulfil the verse (Yeshayahu 30:20): "and your eyes shall see your teachers" (Heikhal Yitzḥak, Oraḥ Ḥayim 9).7

notes_en.en:
Tosefta (Megilla 3:14): "Their faces towards the people and their backs towards the sacred", and so several Rishonim quoted it, among them: the Rif; the Rambam (Laws of Prayer 11:4) and the Rosh (Megilla 3:11). It is implied that the elders turned their backs to the sacred. However, one can interpret that "their backs towards the sacred" means towards the side on which the Holy Ark was, but not that they actually turned their backs to the Holy Ark. And so the Me'iri explained (Megilla 25b), and so it is described in Responsa Ḥatam Sofer (Oraḥ Ḥayim 29; 35). However, from the wording of Rabbeinu Yeruḥam (2:3, page 20a) and the Ran (on the Rif, Megilla 14a), it is implied that they sat with their backs to the Holy Ark, and apparently there were places where they were accustomed so, perhaps because the Holy Ark filled the whole wall at the front of the synagogue.
In the ancient book 'The Differences Between the People of the East and the Land of Israel' it is brought that in Babylonia they were accustomed as explained in the Tosefta, whereas in the Land of Israel they were accustomed otherwise. Similarly, in the days of the Rishonim, in many communities in Ashkenaz they were not accustomed as explained in the Tosefta. And likewise in North Africa and Yemen there were many communities that were not particular about this. The Levush (Oraḥ Ḥayim 150:5) explained that they were not accustomed so because they sold all the seats. And the Taz 2 and the Mishna Berura 14 brought his words. It is further possible that because choosing the elders who would sit at the front of the synagogue is liable to cause disputes, they refrained from it, like the enactment of the Sages that a kohen is called up first, even when there are people more honoured than he, for the sake of the ways of peace (Gittin 59a; below 15:8). In the book Ha-Maspik Le-Ovdei Hashem, chapter 25, he wrote in rebuke of rabbis who are arrogant, that it is not fitting that they sit at the front of the synagogue. And R. Ḥayim Palagi (Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 11:27) wrote that in Izmir they were accustomed that the sages sat by the entrance, and explained that perhaps they were accustomed so in order to prevent light-minded people from sitting by the entrance in a way that sitting in the synagogue looks like a burden to them, and perhaps because all the worshippers were accustomed to kiss the hands of the rabbis, and they did not want to trouble them to walk all the way to the front of the synagogue.
In recent generations, in a gradual process, in many synagogues in the Land people stopped seating rabbis at the front of the synagogue. Apparently the main reason for this is: the disappointment of many members of the public with the conduct of rabbis who, out of great anxiety for preserving tradition, established many safeguards, and in the course of this cancelled sanctified mitzvot and values. Thus it happened that there were rabbis who opposed the fulfilment of the mitzva of settling the Land and the mitzva to defend the people and the Land through enlistment in the IDF, and opposed the study of science and belittled the value of work and of derekh eretz, which preceded the Torah, and some of them stirred up disputes about this. In this situation there were some who preferred that the rabbis deal with religious services such as the kashrut of food, marriage and divorce, the mikveh and the eruv, and not receive an honoured place, which they might perhaps use to stir up disputes and harm sanctified values. For this reason there are communities that do not wish to appoint a rabbi. But the solution is not to cancel the status of the Torah sages, but to take care that they be sages who emphasise the whole range of values in the Torah. To ensure that this will be so, I added the advice to seat elders in other fields too. I learned this advice from Dr Feingold, of blessed memory, about the custom of Rav Yisrael Ze'ev Gustman, of saintly memory, who seated in the 'mizraḥ' of the Netzaḥ Yisrael yeshiva also Torah-observant professors: Prof. Menaḥem Elon, Deputy President of the Supreme Court; Prof. Halperin of physics. He also asked Prof. Yisrael Aumann (who later received the Nobel Prize in economics) to sit in the mizraḥ, but out of humility he preferred to sit with the rest of the public. Rav Gustman explained to those who asked him: "Here in the Land of Israel we must take care of the kingship, and these are people who symbolise the kingship". The kingship, in his words, expresses the various systems on which the nation is founded.

sections.body_en:
On Shabbatot and festivals many women come to pray in the synagogue, and there are righteous women who come to pray even on weekdays. And from the days of the sages of the Mishna it is related of righteous women who came to pray in the synagogue every day and merited long life (above 12:1).

For the sake of modesty, Israel are accustomed to separate between men and women in the synagogue. Therefore Israel are accustomed to build in every synagogue a special place for women, which is called the 'ezrat nashim' (women's section), like the Women's Court in which they held the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing in the Temple, concerning which the Sages said (Sukka 51a) that they made a 'great enactment' in the separation between women and men. "At first the women were inside and the men outside, and they came to light-headedness. They enacted that the women would sit outside and the men inside, and still they came to light-headedness. They enacted that the women would sit above (in a gallery) and the men below". By this they prevented mingling between men and women, and also kept the men from looking at the women (Rambam in his Commentary on the Mishna, and the Rid, Sukka there). And if they did so at a time of song at the Rejoicing of the Water-Drawing, and likewise at a time of eulogy (Sukka 51b, based on Zekharya 12:12), all the more so must this be done at a time of prayer, in which the worshippers need to purify their thoughts and unify their hearts for the service of God, and to remove anything that is liable to distract them from the prayer (Ḥatam Sofer part 5, Hashmatot 190).

Therefore people are accustomed to make a partition (meḥitza) between the men and the women. And they are accustomed to arrange the partition in such a way that the women near the partition can see in a general way what is happening in the synagogue, such as the opening of the ark, the carrying of the Torah scroll and the lifting of the Torah. For this purpose, some are accustomed to make the partition opaque in its lower part, and towards face height they make a partition that is not opaque, so that they can see through it. There are places where people are lenient and rely on the rabbis who hold that a partition may be even ten handbreadths. There are places in which many women come to the prayer, and they set the women's section parallel to the men's section, so that they can hear the ḥazan and the Torah reader well. Ideally, for the sake of modesty, a separate entrance is installed for the women's section.

Concerning the custom of the partition and the separation between men and women in the synagogue, sharp disputes arose between the religious keepers of tradition and the Reform and Conservative, until the custom of the partition became one of the symbols of a community's faithfulness to halakha.8

notes_en.en: See Oraḥ Mishpat (of Rav Kook, 35). According to the Igrot Moshe (Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:39-43), the main reason is that there should be no mingling between men and women, and not because of the concern that the men will look at the women, and therefore the obligation is that the partition reach shoulder height; and so wrote the Seridei Esh (1:8). And many held that the partition must reach above the head in order to prevent looking (Tzitz Eliezer 7:8; Mikveh Ha-Mayim part 4, Yoreh De'ah 26; Aseh Lekha Rav 3:40; Az Nidberu 13:67). And some hold that the main thing in the separation must be a change of domain, and therefore in case of need even a partition of only ten handbreadths suffices (Benei Banim 1:1-3), and that Rav Soloveitchik permitted this in a pressing situation. Until here. In various places, mainly abroad, people rely on this view.

sections.body_en:
It is right to set the entrance of the synagogue opposite the Holy Ark, so that those who are accustomed to bow slightly on entering the synagogue will bow towards Jerusalem and the Holy Ark (Shulḥan Arukh 150:5). And if they wish, they may make further entrances at the sides of the synagogue, but they should try that the main entrance be opposite the Holy Ark.

People are accustomed to build an entrance hall before the doorway of the synagogue, so that those entering the synagogue will first enter the entrance hall, and there they can hang coats and put down belongings, and afterwards they will enter the synagogue. Some learned this from the Yerushalmi (Berakhot 5:1), that one who enters the synagogue "must enter within two doors", as it is said (Mishlei 8:34): "Happy is the man who listens to me, watching daily at my doors". And like the Temple, where they entered the Heikhal through the Ulam (Baḥ, Oraḥ Ḥayim 90:13; Magen Avraham 35). It thus turns out that a person enters the synagogue through two doorways – in his entry through the first doorway into the entrance hall he separates from the affairs of the world outside, and in his entry through the second doorway into the synagogue he devotes himself to cleave to God in prayer (Maharal, Netiv Ha-Avoda 5).

It is good to install near the entrance hall a sink for washing hands, so that people can wash their hands in it before prayer, and so that the kohanim can wash their hands in it before the Priestly Blessing. And it is good that toilets be set up near the entrance hall for those who need to relieve themselves before the prayer or during it.

It is the custom of Israel to make windows for the synagogue (Shulḥan Arukh 90:4), as the Sages said (Berakhot 34b): "A person should pray only in a house that has windows". And as it is related of Daniel, that despite the king's decree not to pray, he prayed to God three prayers every day in the upper chamber facing the windows that were open towards Jerusalem, as it is said (Daniel 6:11): "and his windows were open in his upper chamber towards Jerusalem", and for this he was seized and thrown into the lions' den. The windows are beneficial for prayer, because through them the worshipper, when he pauses for a moment from his prayer, can lift his eyes to heaven and arouse his kavana (Rashi), and through the windows that are open towards Jerusalem he can also be aroused to direct his heart to Jerusalem (Rambam). In addition, through the windows light and air enter the synagogue, and the mind of the worshipper is settled (Rabbeinu Yona). However, when the windows face the street, they must be raised so that they will not cause the worshippers to look at what is happening in the street and distract them from the prayer (Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 27).

It is good to make for the synagogue twelve windows corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel (Zohar part 2, 251a). And some of them should be towards Jerusalem (Mishna Berura 90:9). And even if they add more windows, they have not lost the enhancement of the twelve windows (Eshel Avraham of Butshash 90:5). If the sun dazzles through the windows, comfortable and attractive curtains should be installed for them.

It is right to be diligent about the beauty of the synagogue, and together with this to take care that it be comfortable for the worshippers. For this purpose one should buy comfortable and attractive benches. Likewise, one should install an air-conditioning system for heating in winter and cooling in summer, and pay attention that it not be noisy and disturb the prayers and the sermons. It is permitted to plant trees in the courtyard of the synagogue (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 15:11).

The Sages said (Megilla 28a) that one may not use the roof of the synagogue for weekday needs, such as spreading fruit on it to dry. And although this is done outside the synagogue, since it appears to all as a disgrace to the synagogue – it is forbidden (Biur Halakha 151:12, s.v. 'Yesh').

Sometimes they built an upper storey (an additional floor) above the synagogue, and the Rishonim ruled that one should not use it for disgraceful uses, such as setting up a place to sleep there, and all the more so one should not install toilets there (Maharam of Rothenburg; Shulḥan Arukh 151:12). Likewise we learned (in halakha 4) that it is forbidden to build a house higher than the synagogue; all the more so one should not build an apartment above the synagogue (Ritva, Shabbat 11a). However, weekday uses that have no disgrace in them may be done in the upper storey above the synagogue, but above the Holy Ark it should not be used at all (Mishna Berura 151:40).

All this applies to a building that was built as a synagogue, but if the building was built as an apartment block, and only afterwards one of the apartments was bought for the purpose of a synagogue – the apartments above it were not sanctified, and there is no restriction at all on the residents above the synagogue (Rema, based on the Mahari Weil). However, many Aḥaronim were concerned about the spiritual danger in this, and wrote that one who wishes to guard his soul should keep away from living above the synagogue (Knesset Ha-Gedola; Taz 151:4; Magen Avraham 18; Mishna Berura 42. And in Mishpetei Uziel part 3, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19, he forbade it). According to the view of those who hold that one should not live above a synagogue, it is forbidden to set up a synagogue in an apartment that has apartments above it, for thereby one harms the owners of the apartments above the synagogue.

On the other hand, the Rambam (Responsa Pe'er Ha-Dor 74) was lenient to live even in an apartment built above a synagogue, and wrote only that above the place of the Holy Ark one should not sleep and should not put down work tools. And the Ḥida wrote in practice that one need not be concerned about spiritual danger when living above the synagogue, because all the poskim who were stringent about this did not see the responsum of the Rambam, and had they seen it they would have retracted (Birkei Yosef 151:10; Ḥayim She'al part 1, 56). And so it is right to conduct oneself in practice, because with all spiritual concerns, one should be less concerned in our days (see Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 26:11-12; 19:14).9

Sometimes there is a need to set up a small minyan in an apartment in a shared building for an elderly or disabled person and the like, and those setting up the minyan must comply with the accepted rules of use in residential buildings. It stands to reason that as long as the minyan is small and quiet, and those coming to pray try not to make noise, it complies with the rules of use according to the law.

notes_en.en:
Although the Rambam did not write that the permission is for a pressing situation, one must say so, since ideally it is forbidden to build an apartment higher than the synagogue; therefore the case is one of a pressing situation, in which they were forced to build an apartment above the synagogue. And it is also known that the Muslims forbade the establishment of new synagogues, and many times they set them up on a ground floor in a way that appeared temporary.
It should be added that the words of those who are stringent were said concerning the apartment above the synagogue, but the apartments on higher floors, even though they are directly above the synagogue, have no concern at all, and even above the place of the Holy Ark it is permitted to use them for sleeping and the like (Ikrei Ha-Dat, Yoreh De'ah 26:38; Yabi'a Omer part 6, Oraḥ Ḥayim 26; Aseh Lekha Rav 5, Ketzarot 35). Moreover, in the past, when each house had more distinctiveness and they did not build many storeys, the apartment above the synagogue was noticeable and known as an apartment above a synagogue; but in our apartment blocks there is no indication that it is an apartment above a synagogue, and consequently it is possible that even according to those who are stringent, the spiritual concern diminishes even on the floor above the synagogue.

sections.title_en: 10. Commemorating Donors and the Law of an Apostate Jew
sections.body_en:
A donor who made a significant donation to the building of the synagogue, and wishes it to be noted on a plaque, his wish should be fulfilled, in order to publicise those who perform the mitzva. And so many are accustomed ideally, so that donors will increase. Similarly the Rashba ruled (Responsa 1:581) that when a wealthy man enlarged the synagogue with his money on land of his own, and asked that they write his name on the doorway – his wish should be fulfilled. Both because it concerns his own land, and because such is 'the measure of the sages' and 'the measure of the pious', "in order to give reward to those who do a mitzva… and if the Torah did so (publicising those who do the mitzva), we must follow the measures of the Torah, which are ways of pleasantness" (Rema, Yoreh De'ah 249:13; Magen Avraham, Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:23; Mishna Berura 59; Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 23:7).

It is fitting that the commemorative plaque be modest and not ostentatious, and thereby the donor and the one commemorated will merit true honour and their merits will increase.

Some say that one does not accept donations to a synagogue from an apostate Jew who sinned with idolatry. This is because the synagogue is called a 'small sanctuary', and just as one does not accept a sacrifice in the Temple from an apostate Jew, so one should not accept donations to the synagogue from him (Mahari Weil; Rema, Yoreh De'ah 254:2; Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:11; Ḥatam Sofer). However, it is permitted to accept charity from him, for although he sinned with a very grave sin, one should not withhold from him mitzvot through which his merits will increase. And some say that it is specifically a donation of objects that is not accepted from him, because it bears a resemblance to a sacrifice, but money for the needs of the synagogue – is accepted (Mishna Berura 154:48).

On the other hand, some say that it is permitted to accept any donation from an apostate Jew without any restriction, for the Torah forbade accepting from him only a sacrifice, but one should not prevent him from the other mitzvot, and the more he increases his merits the better (Mabit, and the Shakh 254:5). And so is the prevalent custom (Maharsham in Da'at Torah, Oraḥ Ḥayim 610). However, if he donates a large donation and wants a commemoration, for the honour of the synagogue it is preferable that the name of his parents be written on it.10

notes_en.en:
Those who are stringent not to accept donations to a synagogue from an apostate Jew are: Mahari Weil 67 and the Rema (Yoreh De'ah 254:2; Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:11). In the Shevut Ya'akov (3:85) he was stringent even not to accept charity for the poor from an apostate. However, in general, even those who are stringent agree that charity is accepted from an apostate, for on the contrary, it is good that his merits increase. And only donations to the synagogue are not accepted from him, because of their resemblance to a sacrifice for the Temple. And so wrote the Glosses of the Ḥatam Sofer (to Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 154), that the law of an apostate is the reverse of a gentile: from a gentile charity is not accepted and a sacrifice is accepted, and from an apostate Jew charity is accepted but not a sacrifice or donations to the synagogue. And some hold like the view of those who are stringent concerning objects that resemble a sacrifice, but permit accepting a monetary donation, for example for the writing of a Torah scroll, as brought in Sefer Ḥasidim 687 (Magen Avraham 154:18; Eliya Rabba 154:17; Ḥayei Adam 17:52; Mishna Berura 154:48). And the Maharam Schick (Yoreh De'ah 231) permitted accepting a monetary donation that mixes with other monetary donations to the synagogue. And in the Dovev Meisharim (3:95) he wrote that even according to those who are stringent about a monetary donation for building a synagogue, a donation for building a study hall is accepted.
The Magen Avraham wrote (154:18) that the law of one who desecrates Shabbat publicly is like the law of an apostate. And so wrote the Mishna Berura (154:48), and wrote that the same is the law of one who commits transgressions to provoke. According to the Yafeh La-Lev (Yoreh De'ah 281:5; 254:4), one should not accept donations to the synagogue from an apostate to idolatry, but from one who desecrates Shabbat publicly it is permitted to accept, and only when there is a concern that disgrace will result from his donation – one should not accept. Until here. And so agreed the Sedei Ḥemed (Ma'arekhet Mem, rule 156). And the great rabbis ruled that in recent generations ordinary Shabbat desecrators are not considered apostates (see Peninei Halakha, Kashrut 29:13). And only from one who converted out of his religion, or from a transgressor who sins to provoke, one should not accept, according to those who are stringent.
On the other hand, some are lenient and hold that only a sacrifice is not accepted from an apostate Jew, but donations to the synagogue or charity for the poor are accepted, for there is no aim to diminish his mitzvot and merits; on the contrary, the more he increases mitzvot the better. So wrote the Responsa Mabit (2:214) and the Shakh (254:5). And so it is implied by Sefer Ḥasidim 687, that only when disgrace may result from it should one not accept. And many mentioned both views, and in practice the prevalent custom is to be lenient, as the Maharsham wrote (Da'at Torah, Oraḥ Ḥayim 610).
In the Responsa Beit Yisrael (Landau, Oraḥ Ḥayim 26) he was lenient to accept donations from an apostate even though he earns money through desecrating Shabbat. Until here. It appears that there is no impediment to mentioning the donor on a commemorative plaque even when he does not keep Shabbat, but if he is an apostate to idolatry it is preferable to refrain; however, it is possible to write the names of his parents, and that the donation was donated for the elevation of their souls by their son, without mentioning his name. Similarly the Dovev Meisharim wrote (3:95) concerning a Shabbat desecrator who wanted to donate for the elevation of his father's soul.
The Responsa Aseh Lekha Rav (8:55) wrote that one must be precise in commemoration, and one should not inscribe someone who donated most of a bima in a way that appears as though he donated all of it.
The Torah forbade accepting as a sacrifice an animal that a harlot received as a hire for her payment, or an animal that was exchanged for a dog, because of the disgrace in this. As it is said (Devarim 23:19): "You shall not bring the hire of a harlot, or the price of a dog, into the house of the Lord your God for any vow, for both of these are an abomination to the Lord your God". As a continuation of this the poskim wrote that by rabbinic law one should not accept the hire of a harlot or the price of a dog as a donation to the synagogue. But it is permitted to accept a monetary donation from a harlot, for only a specific object that she received as payment for her sin is considered a hire and is forbidden (Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:21). It appears that it is forbidden to accept charity from criminals who amass their wealth from criminal acts, so as not to lend a hand to their grave crimes against others and against society as a whole.

sections.title_en: 11. Donations from Gentiles and Commemorating Them on a Plaque
sections.body_en:
Just as every gentile, even one who serves idolatry, may volunteer to offer a burnt-offering in the Temple (Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 5:3), so it is possible to accept from him a donation to a synagogue, such as a donation for the purchase of a lamp (Arakhin 6a; Tosafot, Bava Batra 8a; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 259:4; Rema 254:2).

However, it is forbidden to accept charity for the poor from gentiles, both because there is a desecration of God's Name in Israel being forced to make their living from gentiles, and because charity atones for sin, and perhaps by its merit their sin will be atoned and they will be able to continue to subjugate Israel. But donations to the synagogue are accepted, for they are not intended for atonement (Hagahot Asheri; Taz 254:4). And there is no desecration of God's Name in this but a sanctification of God's Name, for by his donation he wishes to share with Israel in the service of God. However, one must take care that he donate with the intent of the Jews who receive his donation, so that it will be clear that he did not intend to consecrate it to the Temple or, alternatively, for the sake of idolatry (Shulḥan Arukh 259:4; Taz 7).

The Sages further warned that if the gentile designated his donation for a specific thing, such as a lamp for the synagogue, its designation should not be changed without his consent, for there is concern that if they change it, he will be resentful towards the Jews for having misappropriated his donation, and a desecration of God's Name will result. However, if a Jew donated money for a lamp, and a lamp is no longer needed, since presumably he trusts the gabbaim, they are permitted to change it and buy with his donation another object of mitzva that is needed (Arakhin 6b; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 259:3).

As for a donation to a yeshiva, if it is intended for the support of the students and the avrekhim, it is considered charity, which it is forbidden to accept from gentiles. And when the donation is for the building, it is like a donation to a synagogue, which may be accepted from gentiles (Va-Yeshev Ha-Yam 2:16; Mishneh Halakhot 5:178; see Da'at Kohen 132, and Peri Ha-Sadeh 2:49).

In general, it is permitted to mention on a commemorative plaque the name of a gentile who donated a large donation to the synagogue. And some are concerned, ideally, about making a plaque for a gentile in the synagogue, lest there be in this an affront to the honour of Israel, that they did not donate enough by themselves. In practice, the rabbi of the place must decide this.11

notes_en.en:
Simply, it is permitted to accept from a gentile a donation of a specific object for the synagogue, as explained in Arakhin 6a; and likewise to commemorate the name of the gentile donor in the synagogue. And some say that their name should not be inscribed in the synagogue (Responsa Yad Yitzḥak 3:271). And some say that ideally one should not accept a specific object from gentiles lest the gentile boast of it in the future and it be called by his name; rather, only a monetary donation for the synagogue as a whole is permitted (Responsa Zikhron Yehuda, Grunwald 56). In practice, if the rabbi of the synagogue holds that there is a sanctification of God's Name in it or an important need for the community, it is possible ideally to inscribe the names of the donors. From missionary organisations it is of course forbidden to accept donations. However, from Christians who have taken upon themselves not to entice Jews to convert to Christianity it is permitted to accept a donation to a synagogue.
Ideally one should not make a synagogue out of a church that has fallen out of use, and after the fact, if they did so, it is possible to pray in it, as explained in Peninei Halakha, Emuna U-Mitzvoteha 10:10. It is further explained there in note 10 that it is permitted to buy for the synagogue chairs that served a church, but lamps are forbidden, since they are considered ornaments of idolatry.
